rationale: Maintenance health is a fair question for an open GitHub skills collection, but the evidence pack never shows release cadence, issue triage, or merged community pull requests. The GitHub items only cover install instructions and skill descriptions. The runtime probe confirms the repo can be fetched and installed, which says nothing about how actively it is maintained.

The repo ships a dedicated meta-skill, skill-creator, for creating, iterating on, benchmarking and optimizing skills, plus a template SKILL.md and a formal Agent Skills spec covering frontmatter rules and directory layout. Packaging and distribution are documented through plugin manifests, local `--plugin-dir` testing, marketplaces and Skills API upload; a runtime probe confirmed skill-creator installs cleanly, and a community user reports having Claude Code create and organize skills. Missing for 10: a hands-on recorded run of an agent using skill-creator to author AND package a new skill end to end (the probe only installed the meta-skill), and explicit evidence that skill-creator itself handles the packaging step.

A recorded hands-on probe ran a fully non-interactive install end to end: `npx -y skills add anthropics/skills --skill skill-creator -a claude-code -y --copy` fetched the repo, installed one skill into ./.claude/skills/ and read it back, with no account needed. First-party docs back this up: a skill is just a SKILL.md directory that Claude picks up once placed on disk, skills can be uploaded via the Skills API, and the Agent SDK can load plugins programmatically. Missing for 10: a first-party documented headless install CLI (the probe used third-party `skills` tooling, and `/plugin install` is an in-session slash command), and explicit docs on unattended or no-prompt plugin installs.

Live probes confirm a working llms.txt at code.claude.com/llms.txt. They also confirm that docs pages are served as raw markdown (e.g. skills.md) with an embedded pointer telling agents where to fetch the full documentation index. The platform skills guide is likewise published as .md, and the skills themselves are spec-conformant SKILL.md files that third-party tooling installed and read cleanly. Missing for 10: no probe confirming an llms.txt for the platform.claude.com API docs or an llms-full.txt bundle, and no independent community report of agents being pointed at these docs.

Skills are positioned to let Claude analyze user data. The repo cites "analyzing data using your organization's specific workflows", and pre-built xlsx/pdf skills let Claude read and extract tables from spreadsheets and documents; a community user praises the xlsx skill's handling of edge cases. However, Skills is an extension mechanism for Claude rather than a dedicated insights feature, and users report that skills often fail to trigger automatically. Missing for 10: a documented first-party data-insights or suggestions workflow, examples of generated insights or recommendations from user data, and hands-on corroboration of analysis quality.

Skills package repeatable workflows ("automating personal tasks") that Claude can load on its own when relevant, and the surrounding Claude Code tooling offers background sessions (agent view), headless `claude -p` runs, plugins bundling hooks, and the Agent SDK for programmatic runs. However, nothing documents a skill itself being scheduled or triggered to run unattended in the background, and community reports say automatic skill invocation is unreliable (in one cited eval the skill was never invoked in 56% of cases). Missing for 10: native scheduling/trigger-based background execution of skills, documentation tying skills to unattended automation, and reliable autonomous invocation.

Skills exist so users can hand tasks to Claude, the built-in assistant. Claude loads a skill when it judges it relevant, or the user invokes one directly with `/skill-name` (docs-2, docs-25). Bundled skills like `/run` and `/verify` work without setup (docs-5), and skill-creator has Claude author and improve skills itself (docs-13). Hands-on community reports say automatic invocation is hit-or-miss, and Vercel's evals found the skill was never invoked in 56% of cases, so users often must trigger skills explicitly (comm-12, comm-13, comm-14). missing for 10: reliable automatic delegation without explicit invocation, independent corroboration of end-to-end task delegation quality.

Skills can be used without an interactive UI in several documented ways. The Messages API takes up to 20 skills per request via the `container` parameter, managed through the Skills API (docs-10, docs-23, docs-24). The Agent SDK lets code control and load skills and plugins (docs-63, docs-78, docs-77). Claude Code supports non-interactive `claude -p` piping (docs-83). A recorded probe also installed a skill non-interactively with `npx skills add ... -y`, with no account needed (probe-rt-1). Missing for 10: an explicit CI integration guide (e.g., a GitHub Actions recipe for skills), and hands-on evidence of a skill actually executing headlessly in a CI pipeline.

MCP integration lives in the host rather than in Skills itself. Claude Code connects to external MCP servers (docs-57, docs-81), with admin controls over which servers run (docs-82). The plugin packaging that distributes skills can also bundle MCP servers alongside skills (docs-6, docs-70), and the Agent SDK supports MCP-backed custom tools (docs-89). Community notes that skills complement MCP and can serve as light instructions for using it (comm-10, comm-16). missing for 10: a Skills-native mechanism for a SKILL.md to declare or wire up MCP servers, documentation of MCP inside the Skills spec or Skills API, and hands-on corroboration of a skill driving MCP tools.

Anthropic Skills is a skill format, open standard, and repository rather than an agent, so publishing an official MCP server is a plausible capability and the axis applies. The evidence does not show one. MCP mentions are client-side: Claude Code connects to MCP servers, plugins can bundle third-party MCP servers, and the Agent SDK offers an in-process MCP server for your own custom tools. None of these is an official MCP server that serves Skills to other agents.

Anthropic documents that Claude loads skills when a natural-language request matches a skill's description, with explicit `/skill-name` invocation as a fallback (docs-2, docs-25, docs-17, docs-32), and that skills can be created conversationally via skill-creator (docs-13, docs-30). Hands-on reports concretely contradict the automatic triggering: users say skills are not invoked from expected prompts and must be named explicitly, sometimes failing even when asked (comm-12, comm-13), and Vercel's cited evals found the skill was never invoked in 56% of cases (comm-14). Missing for 10: reliable invocation from natural-language prompts alone, and independent evidence that triggering works as documented.

Skills are driven from Anthropic's official Claude Code terminal CLI. In-session commands such as `/plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills` and `/plugin install document-skills@anthropic-agent-skills` install skills, `/skill-name` invokes them, and `--plugin-dir` and `claude -p` cover local testing and scripted use. However, this is the host agent's CLI rather than a dedicated Skills CLI, and the one standalone installer shown (`npx skills add`) is third-party tooling. Missing for 10: a first-party standalone CLI for creating, validating, uploading and versioning skills (that management is only exposed via the Skills API), and independent hands-on corroboration of the official CLI workflow.

First-party docs describe a public programmatic surface for Skills. The Skills API uploads and manages custom skills, and a Skill Versions API handles versioning. Skills are attached in Messages API requests via the `container` parameter (up to 20 per request, by `skill_id`/`version`), and the Agent SDK lets code control which skills sessions can invoke and load plugins programmatically. Missing for 10: independent or hands-on corroboration of driving skills through the API, and endpoint-level detail beyond create and versions.

Anthropic Skills is a format and library for packaging agent instructions, scripts, and resources as SKILL.md folders. Issuing scoped or least-privilege API credentials is an auth and identity capability of the services an agent calls, which falls outside what a skill-packaging standard does. Nothing in the pack shows Skills issuing credentials; subagent tool permissions belong to Claude Code, not to Skills, and are not API credential issuance.

The official Claude Agent SDK, programmable in Python and TypeScript, can control which skills sessions invoke, discover filesystem-authored skills, and load plugins and other Claude Code features programmatically (docs-84, docs-63, docs-64, docs-77, docs-78). On the API side, skills are passed via the Messages API `container` parameter (up to 20 per request) and managed through a Skills API with version management (docs-10, docs-23, docs-24, docs-72). missing for 10: independent or hands-on corroboration of building with the official SDKs (the runtime probe used third-party `npx skills` tooling, not an official SDK), and explicit evidence of client-library (non-REST) bindings for the Skills upload/version API.

Skills is an extension and packaging ecosystem with a Skills API and plugin marketplaces, so webhook event subscription is a plausible platform capability and the axis applies. The pack never documents any webhook or event-subscription mechanism. The 'hooks' it mentions in plugins and the Agent SDK are local lifecycle callbacks for blocking operations, not outbound webhooks.

Anthropic Skills is exposed through a Skills API, so an interactive API reference is a fair question for this product. However, the evidence only shows links to static API reference pages (Skills API create, Skill Versions API Reference) and machine-readable docs (llms.txt, .md pages). Nothing shows an interactive explorer or runnable, in-browser examples.

The axis applies because Anthropic Skills is exposed through a Skills API for upload, management, and versioning, so a machine-readable spec for that API is a fair thing to ask for. The pack contains no evidence of a downloadable OpenAPI or equivalent spec. The llms.txt and .md documentation endpoints, and the agentskills.io file-format specification, are machine-readable docs or format definitions, not API specs.

On the Claude API, Skills run inside the code execution environment via the `container` parameter (docs-10), which implies an isolated runtime. Plugin skills can also be tested locally with the `--plugin-dir` flag before distribution (docs-41), and skill-creator can benchmark skills (docs-14). None of this explicitly describes a sandbox that keeps production data out of reach. missing for 10: explicit documentation that the execution container is a sandbox isolated from production data/systems, a documented staging or test-environment workflow for skills, and independent or hands-on corroboration of isolation.

The Skills API supports versioning: skills are referenced with a `skill_id` and an optional `version`, and there is a dedicated Skill Versions API for version management. Plugin manifests and marketplaces also carry version tracking. The pack contains no documented deprecation policy, though `.claude/commands/` files are noted as still working. missing for 10: a documented deprecation/sunset policy and timelines, API-level version guarantees or changelog, independent corroboration of version stability.

The official repo ships a documented `template/SKILL.md` with `name: template-skill` and a placeholder description. The Agent Skills spec documents the required format: YAML frontmatter followed by Markdown, `name`/`description` fields with description length rules, and the directory layout. Anthropic's docs and README also describe creating a skill as just a folder with a SKILL.md, and a skill-creator skill helps author new ones. missing for 10: independent hands-on corroboration of authoring a new skill from the template (the runtime probe only verified installing and reading an existing skill's frontmatter), and `name`-field constraints are not detailed in the evidence.

The collection ships an official skill-creator meta-skill, described as "a skill for creating new skills and iteratively improving them". It covers creating, modifying, and measuring skills, including benchmarking with variance analysis and description optimization for triggering accuracy. A template SKILL.md is also provided. A runtime probe confirmed skill-creator installs cleanly from the repo. missing for 10: evidence that the meta-skill guides packaging/distribution of new skills (plugin packaging is documented only as a separate manual workflow), hands-on corroboration of actually using skill-creator to author or improve a skill.

Skills can bundle executable scripts (anthropic-skills-docs-52), and the spec's example PDF skill "merges multiple PDFs" (anthropic-skills-docs-32), so a skill can carry multi-item logic. Separately, the surrounding Claude Code tooling offers piped input, subagents and agent teams that could fan work out across items (anthropic-skills-docs-83, anthropic-skills-docs-79, anthropic-skills-docs-56). None of this is a documented bulk-operation capability of Skills themselves; it is only implied by these building blocks. Missing for 10: an explicit documented bulk/batch operation mechanism, worked examples of applying a skill across many items, and hands-on or independent corroboration of bulk use.

Event-triggered actions come only from adjacent Claude Code features, not Skills itself: plugins can bundle hooks alongside skills (docs-6, docs-70), and SDK hooks can block dangerous operations before they execute (docs-91). Skills' own triggering is a semantic description match (docs-3, docs-17, docs-25), not a deterministic event rule, and users report it is unreliable: skills were never invoked in 56% of Vercel's evals, and users often must invoke them explicitly (comm-12, comm-13, comm-14). missing for 10: documented event types and rule/condition syntax for hooks, deterministic event-to-action configuration within Skills itself, hands-on corroboration that event rules fire reliably.

Scheduling recurring workflows is a fair question for an agent-extension ecosystem that spans Claude Code and the Agent SDK. However, nothing in the pack documents cron-style, recurring or time-triggered execution of skills. The evidence covers only on-demand invocation (automatic relevance-based loading or `/skill-name`), plugins and marketplaces, background session viewing, and programmatic SDK use. None of these establishes a scheduler.

Versioning is documented: plugin manifests carry a version, plugins support versioned releases, marketplaces provide version tracking from git sources, and the Skills API has an optional `version` parameter and a Skill Versions API for version management. Rollback is only implied (pinning an older version via that parameter, or reverting the git-tracked SKILL.md files), and there is no documented review or approval workflow; skill-creator's benchmarking is evaluation, not change review. Missing for 10: a documented review/approval flow for skill changes, an explicit rollback mechanism or guide, and independent hands-on corroboration of version management.

Skills can be discovered through Claude Code plugin marketplaces, which the docs describe as catalogs offering 'centralized discovery' (docs-8, docs-36). The official anthropics/skills repo can be registered as a marketplace, and named skill bundles can then be installed from it (gh-1, gh-4, docs-9). A runtime probe also confirmed selective installation of a single skill from the repo (probe-rt-1). However, the catalog is plugin-level and decentralized (each marketplace is user-added), and there is no evidence of a browsable or searchable listing UI, a central registry, or a leaderboard. missing for 10: documented browse/search interface for marketplace contents, a central public registry or leaderboard of skills, independent corroboration of the discovery experience.

Several items support clean removal indirectly. Skills are self-contained directories (a SKILL.md plus optional scripts, references and assets), and plugins install and load as one unit, so removing a skill largely means deleting one folder or plugin. Docs also mention that skills can be managed in Claude Code and through the Skills API, and that bundled skills can be turned off with `disableBundledSkills`. However, no evidence documents an actual list-installed command or an uninstall/remove workflow. Missing for 10: explicit list-installed command or API, documented plugin uninstall or skill removal command, guarantees against orphaned files or leftover instructions, and hands-on corroboration of clean removal.

The plugin-marketplace docs state that marketplaces provide version tracking and automatic updates, and the anthropics/skills repo can be registered as a Claude Code marketplace and its skills installed through it. Plugins carry a version in plugin.json, and the API side exposes optional skill versions plus a Skill Versions API. This covers the core of the story, but the auto-update claim is a single line with little detail. missing for 10: an explicit documented update command or a description of how and when auto-updates apply, and hands-on or independent corroboration that updates arrive without reinstalling.

Docs reduce skill creation to a single `SKILL.md` file that Claude picks up and can invoke via `/skill-name`. The official repo gives a two-command install path (`/plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills`, then `/plugin install`). A recorded runtime probe completed a real keyless one-command install of a skill into `.claude/skills/` that read back cleanly. Together this supports a very fast path from nothing to an installed skill. Missing for 10: an explicitly labeled step-by-step quickstart page, any timing evidence for the under-five-minutes claim, and hands-on confirmation that the freshly installed skill actually runs inside Claude.

Skills are plain folders: a SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter and markdown instructions, plus optional scripts/, references/ and assets/ directories. A runtime probe installed one skill into ./.claude/skills/ as copied files and read the SKILL.md back cleanly, so every installed file can be inspected afterward. Before installing, the only evidenced route is browsing the public GitHub repo; no documented install flow or command lists a skill's or plugin's files and scripts for review. Missing for 10: a documented pre-install content listing or preview for plugin/marketplace installs, a first-party review/audit workflow for bundled scripts, and independent corroboration of the review process.

Anthropic says its skills follow the Agent Skills open standard, which "works across multiple AI tools" and is meant for cross-platform portability (docs-47, docs-67, agentskills.io spec). A hands-on probe showed the repo's spec-conformant skill folders can be installed by third-party tooling (`npx skills add ... -a claude-code`). However, the only first-party install instructions are for Claude Code's plugin marketplace and Claude.ai/API, and the one non-Claude use found required a developer to build their own model-agnostic adaptation (comm-17). Missing for 10: documented per-harness install instructions for Codex, Cursor and other agents; any demonstrated install into a non-Claude coding agent; a first-party multi-agent installer.

The official repo documents an in-agent marketplace flow: `/plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills`, then `/plugin install document-skills@anthropic-agent-skills` (gh-1, gh-4, docs-9, docs-71). A recorded hands-on probe also installed a skill with an `npx -y skills add anthropics/skills` one-liner into `.claude/skills/`, which Claude Code discovers automatically (docs-1). Missing for 10: the official path takes two commands (register marketplace, then install), not one; the npx one-liner is third-party tooling, not documented by Anthropic; and no evidence directly confirms the skills are active in the next session after install.

Claude Code docs state that skills follow the Agent Skills open standard, which works across multiple AI tools, and Anthropic says it published Agent Skills as an open standard for cross-platform portability. The agentskills.io spec defines the same SKILL.md-plus-folders structure and required frontmatter that Anthropic's skills use, and a hands-on probe installed an official skill with third-party `skills` tooling, no Anthropic account needed, with clean spec-conformant frontmatter. Missing for 10: hands-on evidence of the same skill folder running unmodified in a non-Anthropic agent (the probe targeted claude-code), and documentation of which Claude-specific frontmatter extensions fall outside the portable spec.

The core skill lifecycle is reachable programmatically. Skills can be uploaded and managed through the Skills API, versioned via the Skill Versions API, and attached to Messages API requests through the `container` parameter (up to 20 per request). The Agent SDK can also load plugins and skills, control which skills a session may invoke, and dispatch them by name. Nothing in the evidence shows explicit API parity with the Claude.ai UI, where the example skills are offered to paid plans, and the API imposes a per-request skill cap. Missing for 10: documented UI↔API parity (e.g., enabling/disabling and sharing skills as in Claude.ai), independent hands-on confirmation of Skills API management, absence of API-only limits like the 20-skill cap.

Skills are plain filesystem artifacts: a folder holding a SKILL.md of YAML frontmatter plus Markdown, with optional scripts, references and assets. They follow the published Agent Skills open standard, which is built for cross-platform portability across multiple AI tools. A hands-on probe confirmed third-party tooling installs the official skills with no Anthropic account, and a community developer ported them to a Gemini-based model-agnostic setup, so local skill data is inherently in open, portable formats. Missing for 10: any documented export or download path for skills uploaded through the Skills API or Claude.ai workspaces, and any account-level data export.

The skills source is publicly readable in the anthropics/skills GitHub repo: raw SKILL.md files are fetchable, and a hands-on probe pulled and installed a skill from it with no Anthropic account. Anthropic also says it published Agent Skills as an open standard. However, no item in the pack states the license the repo's code is released under, so the 'open license' half of the story is unconfirmed. Missing for 10: explicit license terms (e.g. Apache/MIT) for the repo and skills, and any evidence on whether proprietary skills like the document skills share that license.

The skill artifacts and their distribution can be self-hosted. Skills are plain filesystem folders under a published open standard (docs-64, docs-47, docs-67). Marketplaces can be served from your own git repos or local paths (docs-36, docs-9, docs-41). A hands-on probe installed an official skill with third-party tooling and no Anthropic account (probe-rt-1), and a developer ran an adapted, model-agnostic version on another model (comm-17). However, the runtime that executes skills is Claude Code or the Claude API, and API skills run in Anthropic's code-execution container (docs-10, docs-24), so the full stack is not self-hostable first-party. Missing for 10: a documented self-hosted runtime or execution environment, an offline or local-model execution path, and first-party self-hosting docs.

The Agent Skills spec requires a `description` field in every SKILL.md that should describe both what the skill does and when to use it. The official template and a spec example follow this, frontmatter can control whether the user or Claude invokes a skill, and skill-creator can tune descriptions for triggering accuracy. However, hands-on reports show activation does not reliably follow the documented description: skills often fail to trigger on expected keywords, and a cited Vercel eval found a skill never invoked in 56% of cases. So the description does not let a developer reliably predict agent behavior. Missing for 10: deterministic or predictable activation matching the documented triggers, enforcement (beyond 'should') that every skill states when it activates, and independent corroboration that descriptions accurately predict behavior.

The spec and docs define a skill as a directory with a `SKILL.md` file: YAML frontmatter plus Markdown, with optional scripts/references/assets folders. Anthropic positions this as an open standard for cross-platform portability. A hands-on probe installed an official skill via third-party tooling with no Anthropic account and read back plain spec-conformant markdown. A community developer also adapted the repo's skills into a model-agnostic setup running on Gemini. Missing for 10: evidence of a named non-Anthropic harness natively loading an unmodified skill folder (the Gemini port required adaptation).

Data residency is a fair question here because Skills includes a hosted component: custom skills are uploaded to and stored in a workspace via the Skills API. Nothing in the evidence documents choosing a storage region or residency for skills or their data. Local filesystem skills and Agent SDK session-transcript mirroring concern where files live or how SDK sessions are stored, not region or residency selection for Skills, so they are not credited.

Anthropic Skills includes a hosted side: skills are uploaded and managed through the Skills API and kept private to a workspace. That makes data-training posture a fair question for this product. However, nothing in the evidence pack covers training opt-outs, data-usage policies, or controls that stop skill content or session data from being used to train models.

Skills can be uploaded to and managed through Anthropic's Skills API as workspace-private resources, so data retention and deletion is a fair question for this product. However, the evidence never documents retention periods, deletion of uploaded skills, or privacy controls. 'Upload and manage' is too vague to count as a retention or deletion capability, and the session-storage item belongs to the Agent SDK, not Skills.

Anthropic Skills ships through Claude Code, the Claude API Skills endpoint, and a plugin marketplace, so a buyer could reasonably ask whether skill usage is tracked and whether they can opt out. The pack contains no evidence of a telemetry or usage-tracking opt-out. The only nearby items cover exporting your own OpenTelemetry traces and disabling bundled skills, and neither is a privacy opt-out from vendor tracking.

Project-local scope is well evidenced: skills live at `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` inside the project, and a hands-on probe installed a skill into `./.claude/skills/` in a scratch project dir, making it committable with the repo. User-global scope is only implied, by plugin docs describing plugins as "reusable across projects" and "shared across projects and teams"; no user-level skills directory or scope-selection flag is documented. missing for 10: documented user-global skills location (e.g. home-directory skills folder), explicit install-scope choice at install time, independent corroboration of global installs.

The pack documents versioning mechanics: a version field in plugin.json, marketplace version tracking and automatic updates, an optional skill version parameter, and a Skill Versions API. None of it shows release notes or a changelog describing what changed in skills before an update. Version numbers alone do not tell a developer what changed, so this applicable capability is unevidenced.

Anthropic documents automatic, context-driven activation: Claude uses skills when relevant and loads the full SKILL.md when it judges a skill relevant (docs-2, docs-3, docs-25). It also provides guidance for engineering descriptions, such as stating what the skill does and when to use it (docs-17, docs-32), plus a skill-creator tool that optimizes descriptions for triggering accuracy (docs-14). Hands-on reports concretely contradict reliable auto-triggering: several users say skills don't fire on expected keywords even with proper YAML and semantic triggers and must be invoked explicitly (comm-12, comm-13), and a cited Vercel eval found the skill was never invoked in 56% of cases (comm-14). Missing for 10: independently verified reliable automatic triggering, and published evidence that description optimization actually improves activation accuracy.

The evidence only partly covers what skills can execute. Skills may bundle executable scripts (scripts/ directory), and on the API they run in the code execution environment. Operators can also control invocation through frontmatter, the disableBundledSkills setting, and SDK controls over which skills Claude can invoke. Nothing in the pack documents a trust model or vetting for third-party or marketplace skills, nor any telemetry or data-collection disclosure for skills. missing for 10: a documented security/trust model for third-party skills and marketplaces, a telemetry/data-collection disclosure, an explicit sandboxing/permission description for skill scripts, and independent corroboration.

A hands-on probe confirmed that a single skill (skill-creator) can be installed from the anthropics/skills collection with `npx skills add --skill`, but that is third-party tooling. The first-party Claude Code path installs plugins "as one unit": the repo marketplace offers grouped bundles (document-skills, example-skills), and disableBundledSkills is all-or-nothing. The API does let you pick individual skills by skill_id per request (up to 20). Missing for 10: first-party per-skill install from the Claude Code marketplace, documented granular selection within a plugin bundle, and selective disabling of individual bundled skills.

The repo's skill-creator skill provides eval tooling: it can "measure skill performance," "benchmark skill performance with variance analysis," and optimize descriptions for triggering accuracy. Nothing in the evidence shows the collection itself keeps test suites, eval sets or CI regression checks for its published skills such as pptx, xlsx, docx and pdf. missing for 10: evidence of maintained per-skill tests or evals in the repo, CI or regression gating on changes, published eval results, independent corroboration.

All three distribution routes in the story are covered. Plugin marketplaces offer centralized discovery, version tracking, automatic updates, and git-repo or local sources, and anyone with access can register one with a single command (docs-8, docs-36, docs-71, docs-9, gh-1). Plugins are documented for sharing with teammates (docs-7, docs-21). Project-level skills live in `.claude/skills/` (docs-33), and a hands-on probe installed a skill from the official repo into `./.claude/skills/` (probe-rt-1). API skills can also be kept private to a workspace (docs-12, docs-24). Missing for 10: explicit docs that committing `.claude/skills/` to version control shares skills team-wide, and evidence of admin-enforced or managed skill distribution across a team.

On the Claude API, skills take an optional `version` in the container parameter and there is a Skill Versions API for version management, so API users can pin a skill version. In Claude Code, plugins carry a version in `plugin.json` and support versioned releases, but marketplaces advertise automatic updates, and nothing documents a way to pin or freeze them. Missing for 10: a lockfile or pinning mechanism for Claude Code plugins and marketplaces, a documented way to disable or gate automatic updates, team-wide rollout control, and independent or hands-on corroboration of version pinning.

The only maintenance signals are indirect. The openai/plugins repo and its curated marketplace manifest were live and fetchable in a 2026-09-06 probe and list current plugins such as Figma, Expo and build-web-apps. OpenAI also documents a submission-and-review portal through which third parties publish plugins. Missing for 10: any evidence of release cadence or recent releases, issue triage activity, and merged community pull requests to the collection repo itself.

The docs define a skill spec (a directory with SKILL.md requiring name and description), a built-in skill creator that interviews the user about triggers and scripts, and a recorder that drafts skills from demonstrations. The `@plugin-creator` meta-skill scaffolds the plugin.json manifest, MCP wiring and a local marketplace entry, and docs describe packaging and ZIP submission. A community user reports building proprietary skills with skill-creator, and a probe installed the plugin-creator skill as a valid portable folder. Missing for 10: hands-on evidence of an agent completing a full author-to-package run with the meta-skill (the probe only verified installation, not authoring).

A hands-on probe shows a headless, promptless skill install: `npx -y skills add openai/plugins --skill plugin-creator -a codex -y --copy` placed a valid skill in ./.agents/skills, which Codex scans automatically. That path relies on third-party tooling, though. Plugin installs go through the interactive `/plugins` browser and need a new session before use. missing for 10: a documented first-party non-interactive install command or flag, confirmation that `$skill-installer` runs without prompts, and a headless plugin install path that needs no session restart.

Probes confirm a live llms.txt at developers.openai.com (HTTP 200) and Markdown versions of the docs pages, such as codex/skills.md, which point to an llms.txt index. There is also a plugins-specific llms.txt at developers.openai.com/plugins/llms.txt indexing MCP, webhook and checkout docs, and the docs are served as .md URLs agents can fetch directly. Missing for 10: no hands-on evidence of an agent actually consuming these docs to complete a plugin-building task, and no first-party guidance on pointing an agent at llms.txt.

Installed plugins let ChatGPT/Codex work directly on the user's connected data and return AI-generated outputs. Documented examples include summarizing Slack channels and drafting replies, working across Drive/Docs/Sheets/Slides, scanning code to confirm vulnerability findings, and Notion research and knowledge capture. A community user also describes a Metabase skill for querying analytics data. missing for 10: explicit documentation of proactive insight/suggestion generation (e.g., dashboards or recommendations) beyond task-level summaries, and independent hands-on corroboration of insight quality on user data.

The evidence only glances at event-driven or autonomous behavior. The plugin docs mention implementing event subscriptions and webhook delivery for a plugin's MCP server, and the plugin layout can include `hooks.json` and plugin-level `agents/`.
